questions.question: What is the difference between a type conversion and a type assertion in Go?
questions.title: Type conversions versus type assertions
questions.direct_answer: A conversion `T(x)` produces a value of type `T` when the language permits conversion from the static type of `x`; it is checked from known types at compile time, though representation changes can lose information. A type assertion `x.(T)` applies only to an interface expression and checks at runtime whether its dynamic value has concrete type `T` or implements interface `T`.

interviewer_intent.testing: Whether conversion, runtime interface inspection, parsing, and possible information loss are distinct.
interviewer_intent.common_mistake: Expecting an assertion to convert the dynamic value or expecting a numeric cast to parse decimal text.
interviewer_intent.to_stand_out: Use one value to show a legal lossy conversion and a failed assertion to the destination type.

sections.title: Quick revision
items: Conversion syntax is `T(x)` and starts from a statically known source type.
Assertion syntax is `x.(T)` and requires `x` to have interface type.
Numeric conversions may truncate or otherwise change represented values.
Use the two-result assertion to handle a possible mismatch safely.
Neither operation is the same as parsing text such as `"42"` into a number.

sections.title: Interview answer
sections.content:
A conversion asks the language to represent a statically typed value as another permitted type. The syntax is `T(x)`. For example, `float64(count)` converts an integer value for floating-point arithmetic, and `[]byte(text)` converts a string's contents into a byte slice. Whether that conversion is legal is determined from the source and destination types during compilation.

A type assertion starts with an interface value. `value.(string)` asks at runtime whether the dynamic value stored in the interface has the concrete type string. When the target is another interface, it asks whether the dynamic type implements that interface. `result, ok := value.(T)` reports failure without panicking; the one-result form panics on mismatch.

For example, converting `int64(300)` to `uint8` is legal but produces 44 because only the low eight bits remain. Asserting an `any` value containing `int64(300)` to `uint8` does not perform that conversion; it fails because the dynamic concrete type is `int64`. Code must first assert `int64`, then deliberately convert if the range policy allows it.

Parsing is a third operation. `int("42")` is not a numeric parse, so text uses `strconv.Atoi` or a related function. I name the operation precisely: conversion changes a permitted representation, assertion discovers an interface's dynamic type, and parsing interprets external text.

sections.title: Three operations answer three different questions
sections.content:
Conversion asks whether one typed value can be represented as another type. Assertion asks what concrete or behavioural value an interface currently contains. Parsing asks whether bytes or text follow an external grammar. Similar-looking end types do not make these operations interchangeable.

Conversions can be statically legal while semantically unsafe, especially when narrowing numbers. Assertions can be statically possible while failing at runtime. Parsing can fail because input syntax or range is invalid. Each boundary needs its own error or validation strategy.

sections.title: Conversion, assertion, and parsing
sections.content:
| Operation | Form | Main check | Failure boundary |
|---|---|---|---|
| Type conversion | `T(x)` | Source may convert to T | Compile error if forbidden; value may lose information |
| Type assertion | `x.(T)` | Interface dynamic type matches T | `ok == false` or panic |
| Text parsing | `strconv.Parse...` | Text follows numeric grammar and range | Returned error |

sections.title: Compare a narrowing conversion with two assertions
sections.content:
```go
package main

import "fmt"

func main() {
    source := int64(300)
    converted := uint8(source)

    var open any = source
    asserted, ok := open.(int64)
    _, wrongType := open.(uint8)

    fmt.Println(converted)
    fmt.Println(asserted, ok, wrongType)
}
```
The conversion produces 44. The `int64` assertion succeeds, while the `uint8` assertion fails rather than converting the value.

questions.question: What happens during numeric type conversion in Go?
questions.title: Numeric conversions and information loss
questions.direct_answer: Go requires explicit conversion between distinct numeric types. Integer narrowing keeps the value modulo the destination width through sign extension and truncation rules, floating-to-integer conversion discards the fractional part toward zero, and integer-to-float conversion may round when the float lacks precision. A non-constant conversion can succeed even when information changes, so validate ranges before narrowing external or domain-critical values.

interviewer_intent.testing: Whether explicit syntax, truncation, rounding, constants, and domain validation are understood separately.
interviewer_intent.common_mistake: Narrowing first and then checking a value whose original high bits have already been lost.
interviewer_intent.to_stand_out: Explain one integer and one floating-point information-loss rule.

sections.title: Quick revision
items: Distinct numeric types normally require explicit conversion.
Narrow integer conversions can discard high-order bits.
Floating-to-integer conversion discards the fractional part toward zero.
Large integers may round when converted to floating point.
Constants must be representable where a typed assignment or conversion requires it.

sections.title: Interview answer
sections.content:
Go makes conversions between distinct numeric types explicit so the source shows where representation may change. The syntax compiles when the language permits the pair, but a successful runtime conversion does not promise mathematical equality. A smaller integer type cannot represent every larger value, and a floating type cannot represent every large integer exactly.

For integer conversion, the value is extended to implicit infinite precision with its sign and then truncated to the destination width, after which it is interpreted as the destination type. That is why `uint8(300)` becomes 44. Floating-to-integer conversion discards the fraction toward zero, so `int(-3.9)` is -3. Integer-to-float and float-to-float conversions may round.

For example, an API can parse a quantity into `int64`, check that it is between zero and 255, and only then convert to `uint8`. Converting first and validating afterward is too late because 256 has already become zero and could look valid. A typed constant that cannot fit the destination is rejected by the compiler, which catches literal mistakes earlier.

I use explicit bounds checks when narrowing data from files, APIs, databases, or calculations. For ordinary widening where every source value is representable, the conversion documents arithmetic intent. For money and exact identifiers, I avoid floating point when rounding would violate the domain.

sections.title: Legality is not the same as losslessness
sections.content:
The compiler verifies that a conversion category is allowed. The programmer verifies that the particular runtime value preserves the required meaning. Those checks differ because runtime values are not always known during compilation.

Validate in the wider source type before narrowing. After truncation, several original values can map to the same destination value, so the evidence needed for a correct range decision has been destroyed.

sections.title: Why validating after conversion is too late
sections.content:
| Stage | Value | Interpretation |
|---|---:|---|
| Source `int64` | 300 | Outside uint8 range |
| Narrow to 8 bits | 44 | High bits discarded |
| Validate converted value | 44 | Looks valid but is wrong input |
| Correct order | Check 0..255 first | Reject 300 before conversion |

questions.question: How do conversions between `string`, `[]byte`, and `[]rune` differ?
questions.title: String, byte-slice, and rune-slice conversions
questions.direct_answer: The two conversions use different units. `[]byte(s)` gives the raw bytes that make up a string, while `[]rune(s)` decodes the string into Unicode code points. Use bytes when the exact encoding matters and runes when you need to work with Unicode characters. Converting either slice back creates a string from those values.

interviewer_intent.testing: Whether exact-byte preservation, UTF-8 decoding, invalid input, and ownership semantics are understood.
interviewer_intent.common_mistake: Converting malformed data to runes before diagnostics, or assuming a byte slice contains one element per character.
interviewer_intent.to_stand_out: Explain which conversion can preserve invalid UTF-8 and why observable string immutability still holds.

sections.title: Quick revision
items: `[]rune(s)` decodes code points and maps invalid UTF-8 to U+FFFD.
`string(bytes)` can contain arbitrary bytes, including invalid UTF-8.
Choose bytes for exact data and runes for code-point operations.

sections.title: Interview answer
sections.content:
A Go string is a read-only sequence of bytes. Converting it to `[]byte` gives those raw bytes in a mutable slice. Converting it to `[]rune` first reads the bytes as UTF-8 and gives one Unicode code point per element.

The difference is visible with `"é"`: `[]byte("é")` has two bytes, `c3 a9`, but `[]rune("é")` has one rune, `U+00E9`. Therefore, bytes are the right unit for files, network data, hashes, and exact encodings. Runes are usually the better unit when a program must inspect or replace Unicode code points.

Both conversions produce a slice that can be changed without changing the original string. Converting `[]byte` back with `string(bytes)` keeps those byte values, even when they are not valid UTF-8. Converting `[]rune` back encodes the rune values as UTF-8; invalid rune values become the Unicode replacement character.

Choose the unit the problem actually uses: bytes for exact encoded data and runes for Unicode code-point operations. A rune is not always one complete user-visible character, because a displayed character can contain more than one code point.

sections.title: First, know what string, byte, and rune mean
sections.content:
A Go `string` stores bytes and is commonly used for UTF-8 text, but the language does not require every string to contain valid UTF-8. A `byte` is an alias for `uint8`, so it represents one raw byte. A `rune` is an alias for `int32` and is used for a Unicode code point.

This is why `len(text)` reports bytes, while `utf8.RuneCountInString(text)` reports decoded runes. Neither count is guaranteed to equal the number of symbols a person sees on screen: one visible symbol can be made from several code points.

sections.title: What information each conversion keeps
sections.content:
`[]byte(text)` keeps the original encoding units. It can preserve malformed UTF-8, which is useful when inspecting network input or a file exactly as received. `[]rune(text)` decodes UTF-8. When decoding finds an invalid byte sequence, the result contains `utf8.RuneError`, so the exact bad bytes are no longer available from the rune slice.

Converting either slice back returns a string, which is again read-only through normal Go operations. Application code should rely on that observable behavior rather than memory sharing: the compiler may avoid a copy only where the program cannot observe a difference.

sections.title: Two paths out of a string
sections.content:
```mermaid
flowchart LR
  A["string: read-only bytes"] --> B["[]byte: preserve raw bytes"]
  A --> C["[]rune: decode UTF-8"]
  B --> D["inspect or change bytes"]
  C --> E["inspect or change code points"]
  D --> F["string(bytes)"]
  E --> G["string(runes)"]
```

sections.title: Preserve encoding bytes or decode one rune
sections.content:
```go
package main

import "fmt"

func main() {
    text := "é"
    bytes := []byte(text)
    runes := []rune(text)
    runes[0] = 'e'
    fmt.Printf("bytes=% x runes=%U changed=%s original=%s\n", bytes, runes, string(runes), text)
}
```
The byte view contains `c3 a9`; the rune view contains one changed code point. The original remains `é`.
